record.paper_title: Open Problems in Geometric Methods for Instance-Based Learning
record.original_question: How can the nearest neighbors of a new query point be computed efficiently?

evidence.quote: How can the nearest neighbors of a new point be computed efficiently?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $(X, d)$ be a metric space and let $P = \{p_1, \ldots, p_n\} \subset X$ be a finite set of $n$ points, given in advance and available for preprocessing. For a positive integer $k$, the $k$-nearest-neighbor problem asks, given a query point $q \in X$, to return a subset $N_k(q) \subseteq P$ of size $k$ such that for every $p \in N_k(q)$ and every $p' \in P \setminus N_k(q)$, $d(q,p) \le d(q,p')$.

Design a data structure that, after preprocessing $P$, answers $k$-nearest-neighbor queries efficiently. Specifically, identify schemes that achieve sublinear query time (ideally polylogarithmic in $n$) using only polynomial space and preprocessing, while remaining effective in high-dimensional Euclidean spaces $X = \mathbb{R}^d$ as well as in general metric spaces. Characterize the best achievable trade-offs among space, preprocessing time, and query time for both exact and $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximate nearest-neighbor search, and determine whether the "curse of dimensionality" — the apparent impossibility of obtaining query time sublinear in $n$ with space polynomial in $n$ and $d$ for exact nearest neighbors when $d$ is large — can be overcome.
artifact.status_search_result: Nearest-neighbor search is a classical problem with substantial progress: kd-trees, ball trees, cover trees, and metric trees give efficient algorithms in low dimensions; locality-sensitive hashing (Indyk–Motwani, Andoni–Indyk) and data-dependent LSH (Andoni–Razenshteyn 2015) give near-optimal approximate solutions in high dimensions. However, exact nearest-neighbor search in high dimensions still suffers from the curse of dimensionality, and tight bounds on the space/time trade-off remain open. The problem is therefore partially solved.

status_evidence.title: Optimal Data-Dependent Hashing for Approximate Near Neighbors
status_evidence.snippet: Andoni and Razenshteyn establish optimal exponents for data-dependent LSH for approximate nearest neighbor search in Euclidean space.
status_evidence.claim: Approximate nearest neighbor in high dimensions has near-optimal known algorithms.

status_evidence.title: Nearest neighbor search - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: Survey of methods including kd-trees, cover trees, LSH; notes the curse of dimensionality for exact NNS.
status_evidence.claim: Many practical and theoretical algorithms exist; exact high-dimensional case remains hard.
